extracted.intended_audience: people interested in ARIPO/Harare Protocol and software patent rules (patent applicants, practitioners, policy advocates, researchers)
extracted.subtask_short: ARIPO Harare Protocol software patent rules
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes the Harare Protocol provisions relevant to patentability (including computer programs) and the procedural relationship between ARIPO and its contracting states. Useful for applicants, practitioners and policy analysts working with ARIPO-region patent filings.

rubrics_metrics.name: ARIPO grant authority (designation-based system)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Harare Protocol empowers ARIPO to grant patents on behalf of the contracting states via a designation-based system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ARIPO acts as a regional patent-granting office; applicants file with ARIPO and designate contracting states where protection is sought. The page lists the contracting states that are members of ARIPO (e.g., Botswana, Ghana, Kenya, Uganda, Zimbabwe, etc.) which determines where ARIPO-granted patents may have effect if not refused by the state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right of contracting states to refuse ARIPO patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Contracting states have the power to refuse patents granted by ARIPO in their individual territory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if ARIPO grants a patent, individual member states may exercise their national power to refuse that ARIPO patent within their jurisdiction. Applicants should consider possible national refusals when assessing regional filing strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coexistence of national legislation with the Harare Protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: All contracting states are allowed to have their own legislations on patents that coexist with the Harare Protocol.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: National patent laws remain relevant alongside ARIPO procedures; applicants and practitioners must consider both ARIPO rules and individual national statutes/regulations which may diverge in scope, exclusions, or procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (novelty, inventive step, industrial application)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(10)(a): ARIPO patents shall be granted for any inventions, in all fields of technology, provided that they are new, involve an inventive step and are susceptible of industrial application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The classic three-part patentability test applies: novelty (newness), inventive step (non-obviousness), and industrial applicability (utility). These are the substantive thresholds an ARIPO patent application must meet to be granted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enumerated non-patentable subject-matter (Section 3(10)(h))
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(10)(h) lists items that shall not be regarded as inventions: (i) discoveries, scientific theories and mathematical methods; (ii) aesthetic creations; (iii) schemes, rules and methods for performing mental acts, playing games or doing business, and programs for computers; (iv) presentations of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is an explicit exclusion list that includes 'programs for computers' among other categories. Whether a specific subject-matter falls within an exclusion depends on interpretation and application to the claimed matter (see the 'as such' limitation below).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'As such' limitation on exclusions and effect for software patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 3(10)(i) states that paragraph (h) (the exclusions) shall exclude patentability only to the extent to which an ARIPO patent application or ARIPO patent relates to such subject-matter or activities 'as such'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'as such' qualifier narrows the exclusion: subject-matter that involves or implements excluded items but goes beyond them (e.g., a computer program producing a technical effect) may still be patentable. The page notes that this wording allows ARIPO to grant software patents, since the exclusion does not categorically ban software-related inventions unless they are claimed 'as such'. Practitioners should draft claims and descriptions to emphasize technical features or industrial applicability to avoid being treated as excluded 'as such'.
